analysis.one_liner: Protects mobilized reservists from eviction, insurance lapses, and job loss during active duty.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to shield reservists called up for the Gulf War from eviction, lapsed insurance, and lost jobs — backed by 9 senators split evenly between the parties — never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill updated the World War II-era law that protects people called to military service. It would have raised the rent ceiling for eviction protection from $150 to $1,200 a month, let deployed doctors and other professionals pause their malpractice premiums, required health insurers to restore coverage without waiting periods, and given every reservist the right to get their old job back. It was introduced in the closing weeks of the 101st Congress and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Reservists and National Guard members called to active duty — a group mobilized in large numbers for the 1990-91 Gulf War buildup — and their families. A servicemember's family could not be evicted from a rental home costing up to $1,200 a month without a court's leave. A deployed nurse, doctor, lawyer, or other professional could suspend malpractice premiums, get a refund for the deployment period, and reinstate coverage afterward with no premium increase. A returning servicemember could get employer health coverage restored with no new waiting period or exclusion for pre-existing conditions. All reservists — not just those on active duty 90 days or less — would gain the right to reemployment after any non-training active duty.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the rent ceiling for eviction and distress protection from $150 to $1,200 a month, so a landlord cannot evict a military family from a typical rental without a court's permission while the servicemember is deployed.

Lets professionals ordered to active duty suspend their liability insurance without paying premiums, get refunds for the suspended period, and reinstate coverage afterward with no premium increase — and pauses any malpractice lawsuit against them until coverage resumes.

Requires reinstatement of health insurance that lapsed during military service, with no waiting period or exclusion for conditions that arose before or during service, covering the servicemember's dependents as well.
Extends reemployment rights to all reservists returning from any active duty other than training, striking the previous limit that covered only those on active duty for 90 days or less.
Extends the Act's power-of-attorney protections to documents that expire after August 2, 1990, matching the current mobilization.

analysis.who_pays: Residential landlords, who could not evict military families in lower-rent units without going to court; professional liability insurance carriers, which had to suspend coverage on request, refund premiums, reinstate without a surcharge, and face lawsuits delayed; and health insurers, which had to restore lapsed coverage and waive waiting periods for returning servicemembers and their families.
analysis.who_pays_short: Landlords and liability and health insurers

drawbacks.text: Malpractice lawsuits against deployed professionals would be frozen, and the statute-of-limitations clock paused, so patients injured before the deployment would wait longer for their day in court.

Insurance carriers bear real costs — refunded premiums, a guaranteed reinstatement period without a premium increase, and coverage restored with no waiting periods — which in practice get spread across their other policyholders through somewhat higher prices.

The eviction protection is capped: it only covers rentals at $1,200 a month or less, and health-coverage protections exclude conditions the government determines to be service-connected, leaving those to the veterans' system instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but narrow: they go to a specific group — people pulled away from jobs, homes, and practices by a war mobilization — and the costs are modest, mainly delayed lawsuits and small premium shifts. An honest supporter would concede that freezing malpractice suits delays justice for injured patients, and that the bill did nothing for the many reservists whose situations fell outside its caps and conditions. It was a targeted patch to a 1940 law, not a broad program — and because it died, reservists mobilized for the Gulf War got none of it from this bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last ten weeks of the Congress and referred to the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee, where it sat — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — until the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Alan Cranston introduced the bill on October 25, 1990, with eight cosponsors split evenly between the parties: four of 55 Senate Democrats (DeConcini, Mitchell, Graham, Akaka) and four of 45 Senate Republicans (Murkowski, Thurmond, Specter, Jeffords).

The bill responded to the Gulf War mobilization then underway: it applied to people ordered to active duty after August 1, 1990, and extended power-of-attorney protection to documents expiring after August 2, 1990 — the day Iraq invaded Kuwait.
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and it died with that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and insurance carriers were spared the new duties the bill would have imposed on them. Mobilized reservists and their families entered the Gulf War without these added protections — a gap that anyone facing eviction, a malpractice premium bill, or a lapsed health policy during deployment paid for.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords and insurers who avoided new duties

for.name: Alan Cranston
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-CA); chairman of the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee, to which the bill was referred
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the final weeks of the Congress; it never advanced past referral to his own committee

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no opposition appears in the record; support at introduction was evenly bipartisan, with 4 of 55 Senate Democrats and 4 of 45 Senate Republicans joining the Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The bill forces carriers to suspend coverage on request for deployed professionals, refund the suspended premiums, and reinstate coverage for at least the policy's remaining term without a premium increase, while malpractice suits against their policyholders are stayed. It protects individual policyholders at the carriers' expense.

Carriers must reinstate lapsed coverage for returning servicemembers and waive waiting periods or exclusions for conditions arising before or during service, for family members too. This removes a standard way insurers avoided paying claims for people who left and rejoined coverage.

Landlords could not evict or bring distress proceedings against military families in units renting for $1,200 a month or less without a court's leave, limiting their ability to regain possession during a deployment.
